revised_comments: Active use of digital/mobile-money payments among Chad's adult population is low. GSMA reporting from November 2025 puts active mobile money usage at around 13% of the population, one of the lowest rates in the CEMAC/Sahel region, compared with 55% in Cameroon and 33% in Nigeria. IMF Financial Access Survey data record around 25 active mobile money accounts per 1,000 adults in 2022, a similarly low level of engagement. The World Bank's Global Findex-based G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators database lists the specific "made or received digital payments in the past year" indicator for Chad as unavailable. Taken together, the evidence indicates active digital payment usage among adults remains below 20%.

Comments: No credible evidence found in accessible sources for refugee/migrant access provisions in Chad digital payments (e.g., KYC exemptions for refugees, UNHCR mobile money programs in Chad). revision_notes: Escalated to full path: light search surfaced a clearly authoritative, Chad-specific source. Fetched Biometric Update (9 May 2025), which reports that Chad's National Commission for the Reception and Reintegration of Refugees (CNARR), National Agency for Secure Documents (ANATS), UNHCR and the World Bank are piloting National Refugee Identification Numbers (NNIRs), issued via the existing biometric SIGPTS platform (built by Idemia), explicitly to let refugees open bank accounts and register phone numbers — previously blocked because CNARR/UNHCR refugee documents were not recognised by banks or telecoms. As of 1 May 2025 about 4,000 NNIRs had been issued in a N'Djamena pilot against a phase target of 7,000 and an eventual national ambition of 25,000+. Corroborated by GSMA (17 Nov 2025), which confirms Chad-specific practical barriers (13% active mobile money use nationally, handset affordability, 1-3% 4G coverage for refugees) and by UNHCR's long-running "Displaced and Disconnected" research programme, which lists Chad among priority countries with ID-linked legal barriers to mobile/financial access. Value code revised from 0 (Unknown) to 2 (Partial): a legal/technical access pathway now exists but is limited to a small pilot, not national coverage.
revised_comments: Refugees and displaced persons in Chad have only partial access to digital payment accounts. Since May 2025, Chad's National Commission for the Reception and Reintegration of Refugees (CNARR), the National Agency for Secure Documents (ANATS), UNHCR and the World Bank have piloted National Refugee Identification Numbers (NNIRs), issued through the country's biometric Integrated Population and Secure Documents Management System (SIGPTS). Refugees receiving an NNIR gain a nationally recognised identifier that financial institutions and telecom operators are expected to accept, addressing a long-standing problem whereby refugee documents issued by CNARR or UNHCR were not recognised for opening bank accounts or registering SIM cards. The pilot, centred on N'Djamena, had issued around 4,000 NNIRs by May 2025 against a phase target of 7,000, with an eventual ambition to cover all refugees aged ten and above (potentially 25,000 or more in the initial phases). Coverage therefore remains partial and geographically limited. Practical barriers compound the legal gap: GSMA reporting notes that active mobile money use across Chad's general population is only around 13%, and that as few as 1-3% of refugees in eastern Chad have 4G coverage, alongside handset affordability and literacy constraints. Access for refugees and migrants is best characterised as partial rather than fully enabled or entirely absent.
